title: Fast Fourier Transform
body:
The [[Discrete Fourier Transform]] computed in $O(N \log N)$ instead of $O(N^2)$. It is not a
different transform; it is the same matrix product organised so the redundant work is done once.
Cooley and Tukey published it in 1965, Gauss had it in 1805, and it is on most lists of the most
important algorithms ever written.

## The idea

Split the input by index parity. Even-indexed samples in one half, odd in the other:

$$
X_k = \underbrace{\sum_{m} x_{2m}\,\omega_{N/2}^{km}}_{E_k}
    + \omega_N^{k}\underbrace{\sum_{m} x_{2m+1}\,\omega_{N/2}^{km}}_{O_k}
$$

Both sums are DFTs of length $N/2$, because $\omega_N^2 = \omega_{N/2}$ (see [[Roots of Unity]]).
Then the periodicity of the roots gives the second half for free:

$$
X_k = E_k + \omega_N^k O_k, \qquad X_{k + N/2} = E_k - \omega_N^k O_k
$$

One multiply and two adds produce **two** outputs. That pair is the butterfly, and it is where the
saving lives: the naive transform computes $E_k$ and $O_k$ afresh for every $k$, and this computes
them once.

## Why $O(N\log N)$

$T(N) = 2T(N/2) + O(N)$: two half-size transforms plus a linear combining pass. That recurrence
solves to $O(N\log N)$, and it is **the same recurrence as [[Merge Sort]]**, for the same reason.
Both split, recurse, and combine in linear time, so both build a recursion tree of depth $\log N$
with $O(N)$ work per level. See [[Time Complexity]] and [[Asymptotic Analysis]], and
[[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] for divide and conquer as a design strategy.

The size of the win is not academic. At $N = 10^6$, $N^2$ is $10^{12}$ and $N\log_2 N$ is about
$2 \times 10^7$: **five orders of magnitude**, the difference between a day and a second. This is
the clearest case in the degree of an algorithm, not hardware, being what made an application
possible.

## What it enables

- **Fast convolution.** By the [[Convolution Theorem]], convolving becomes transform, multiply,
  transform back: $O(N^2)$ down to $O(N\log N)$. Large filters, big-integer multiplication, and
  polynomial multiplication all go this way.
- **Real-time spectral work**: audio equalisers, spectrograms, MP3 and JPEG encoding, radar, MRI
  reconstruction. Every one of them is running this on a stream of samples that
  [[Sampling Theorem]] said were enough.
- The recursion assumes $N$ is a power of two in its simplest form, which is why signal lengths get
  zero-padded to 1024 or 4096. Mixed-radix versions handle other sizes.

Implementations are usually iterative rather than [[Recursion|recursive]], with a bit-reversal
permutation up front and the butterflies applied in $\log N$ passes.
